claims.text: Multi-element alloys at near-equiatomic ratios can form simple single solid-solution nanoparticles.
Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can be synthesized through chemical or physical routes.
Undoped near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles intrinsically undergo diffusion and elemental segregation during high-temperature operation.
Adding a minor amount of a high-melting-point, low-diffusivity dopant suppresses diffusion-driven elemental segregation.
The dopant restricts atomic mobility specifically at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries.
High melting point and inherently low diffusivity make the dopant an effective kinetic barrier to motion of the primary constituent elements.
Reduced atomic mobility can suppress segregated-phase formation and help preserve a homogeneous solid solution.
Severe lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys is associated with low atomic diffusivity.
Doped nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than otherwise identical undoped nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
Doped nanoparticles will retain their solid-solution phase better than undoped nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
The relevant catalytic operating-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric operating-temperature range is 473–1923 K.
Keeping the dopant concentration below a phase-separation threshold will avoid formation of a separate dopant-containing phase while preserving near-equiatomic ratios.
The magnitude of segregation suppression depends on dopant identity, dopant concentration, and nanoparticle synthesis method.
Any resulting functional-performance improvement may vary with dopant identity, concentration, and synthesis method.
